British Columbia Telephone Company important that I make that point clear. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) went into the merits of the bill so fully that it is hardly necessary for me to go over the same ground and perhaps repeat much of what he said. I am sure I could not say it so well or with the same clarity.
There is one point particularly which I wish to draw to the attention of the house. Although this company operates and has almost a complete monopoly on telephone service in the province of British Columbia, there is no control whatsoever over the company except that exercised by the board of transport commissioners with respect to an application for an increase in capital or in tolls. As shown by the report of Messrs. McTaggart and Brakenridge, I am afraid the board of transport commissioners is so far away from British Columbia that its members do not understand the people's needs.
Quite recently there came to my hand a letter which was sent to one of the British Columbia M.L.A.'s by a party on behalf of certain residents in an area in the municipality of Burnaby. The letter drew attention to the fact that in the opinion of the writer the company was discriminating against a certain area in the allocation of telephones. I do not know whether or not there is any merit in the contention, but I want to point out that there is no authority that can investigate such a charge and find out whether or not there is any merit in it. The M.L.A. sent the complaint to the public utilities commission at Victoria, and he received a letter in reply reading:
Dear Sir:
In reply to your letter to the chairman of February 28, I am directed to advise that B.C. Telephone Company is under dominion jurisdiction.
That is all. The public utilities commission could not do anything. After the M.L.A. received that letter, he felt, logically enough, that if there was no authority to supervise the operations of the company in British Columbia there should be in Ottawa where the charter was granted. Therefore he sent me the complaint and I forwarded it to the board of transport commissioners. In due course I received the following letter in reply: Dear Sir:
I am directed to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 16th instant, enclosing copy of petition from the residents of South Burnaby, B.C. regarding allocation of residential telephones, which is returned herewith.
I would point out for your information that the board has never considered that its powers with respect to telephone companies extend to the matter of furnishing or dealing with telephone service. Such powers as the board possesses are
2476	HOUSE OF COMMONS
British Columbia Telephone Company limited to matters affecting the tolls charged for the service. Under the circumstances the board is unable to be of any assistance.
The letter was signed by the acting secretary. I think the reading of these two letters is sufficient reason for not granting to the British Columbia Telephone Company too large an amount of capital at any one time because obviously the only control the people of British Columbia have over the company is when it has to make application here for an extension of capital, or applies to the board of transport commissioners for an increase in tolls. If we at this time authorize the amount of capital that they ask for, $50 million, which according to their way of financing they can increase to $100 million or even more, we are putting all the subscribers of the British Columbia Telephone Company under a severe handicap.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra went over the report made by the committee of investigation appointed by the city council of Vancouver pretty well clause by clause. He pointed out that in the first place the telephone company operates through a licence contract, and that the contract provides for an annual payment by the B.C. Telephone Company of one per cent of its gross operating revenues to the parent company, Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company of Montreal. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out, it was brought out at the time of the application to the board of transport commissioners to increase the tolls that the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company did not provide and did not have the staff to provide any sort of service whatsoever to the people of British Columbia who use the services of the B.C. Telephone Company. Yet for the year 1948 the B.C. Telephone Company made a payment of $181,051 to the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, and it is not shown that any particular service was given in return for that large sum of money. Perhaps I might as well read the pertinent paragraph in the report. It is as follows:
Nevertheless the fact remains that while the B.C. Telephone Company paid to the Anglo Company for services under this contract for the year 1948 the sum of $181,051, the amount Anglo in turn paid to its parent, the Associated Company, for such service for the same year only amounted to $3,150.
Would the hon. member kindly identify the report from which he has read a quotation?
I think I mentioned the report. It is a report prepared by Messrs. McTaggart and Brakenridge.
A report prepared for the city of Vancouver.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join the two hon. members for Vancouver in discussing this bill. I do so because I agree with what they have said. I think the practice is becoming all too prevalent of having bills brought into this house with very little knowledge of what they involve. They are passed, and then two or three years later we get repercussions. There are two things I do not like in the procedure that has been followed in connection with this bill. In the first place, with all due respect to the sponsor of the bill, I think it should have been sponsored by a member from Vancouver.

On a point of order,
Mr. Speaker, in discussing the principle of legislation is it a legitimate argument to mention who happens to introduce the bill in question?
You must have something else to say.

I will before I am through.
That is my first point, and that is why I am speaking tonight. That sort of thing makes me suspicious. If a bill was to be introduced in this house that was in the best interests of the part of the country I represent, I would expect to introduce it. If it is necessary to by-pass me in order to get it
British Columbia Telephone Company before the house, then I think there must be something the matter with it. I am not holding that against the hon. member. He is a very capable member and a good friend of mine, and I would be the last man in this house to suggest that he would sponsor something that was not absolutely legitimate. But I do suspect the motives of those who may be taking advantage of his innocence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the second thing that makes me suspicious, and another reason why I am on my feet, is that this bill came through the back door. It had its origin in another place. That does not reflect on the other place, but if it is necessary for me to visit your home, Mr. Speaker, I will not sneak in the back door; I shall come in the front way, and let you know exactly the purpose of my visit. The procedure is in reverse. Under ordinary circumstances, and for a long time, any bill that came before the House of Commons went through the resolution stage, if it was a money bill, or was introduced by a member of the house. Then, it generally went to a committee of this house which examined it in all its details, and brought it back to this house. I am not in favour of the procedure of having a bill passed through the other place and come in the back door. It is given to the members of this house with very little knowledge of what the implications of that bill are.
It is not as innocent as it sounds, Mr. Speaker. It is merely following up a lot of legislation that is tied up with a great octopus on this North American continent in the telephone business. It has for its purpose, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr- Green) and the hon- member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) suggested, an increase in capital from $25 million to $75 million, an increase of $50 million. Well, that is a lot of money for a little company. It is supposed to be a small company, an innocent little struggling company that is trying to expand its services out into the wilds of British Columbia. It is not so small, and it is not so innocent. It is merely one of the arms of the octopus that stretch out in that particular spot.
I do not want to waste the time of the house, but I have in my hand a chart that sets out exactly what the tie-in is on the North American continent, not in Canada alone, of this innocent, poor little company that has this very innocent, poor little bill before the house. They only want to increase their share capital by $50 million, and in addition to that they want to make a change in the capital structure. They want to break down the value of the shares from $100 to $25; that may not be so innocent as it sounds,

British Columbia Telephone Company either. A lot of widows and orphans, people with a little money, can buy twenty-five dollar shares. After they get enough of these twenty-five dollar shares, someone can buy them all in and own them all overnight, thus squeezing out the little fellow. That has been the history of the development of practically all industries on this continent.
I am not going to read this, but at the top of the chart there is the Associated Telephone and Telegraph Company of the United States, which is tied in with the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, which in turn is tied in with the Bell Telephone Company and some twelve other companies which are tied in with the B.C. Telephone Company. In my opinion there is a complete tie-up, a directive tie-up with the large companies in the United States and Canada. This is not as innocent as it appears. Let us take a look, for a moment, at what happens in the development of this type of organization, and the monopoly position that it holds today. There is no one in this house or in this country who can fool me into believing that the Bell Telephone or the B.C. Telephone or any of these other subsidiaries are just little struggling organizations trying to take care of themselves. It is not so. They have a granddaddy somewhere with a lot of power who is taking very good care of the little family. As the member for Vancouver East has suggested, the company is getting a long way into the pocketbook of anyone who is in a position to take advantage of its service.
What happens when the capital of a company is expanded, as is suggested in this bill? You do not have to go far to find out. We have had lesson after lesson during the lifetime of most of the members in this house, all of them in fact, and in the very organization we are talking about tonight. In my hand I hold a little book entitled "What Price Telephones?" by Norman Perelman. It contains a complete history of the development of these companies in the United States like American Telephone and Telegraph, the granddaddy of them all. Back in 1929, 1930 and 1935, what happened to the employees of that particular organization when it made a large capital expansion and invested a lot of money that did not turn out as well as the company expected? It was not the board of directors or the shareholders that suffered, it was the employees of that organization. I am going to read just a few extracts from this booklet so you will not think I am merely expressing my own opinion. These are the facts as contained in this research pamphlet on the development of telephones on the North American continent, with particular reference to the United States. I use the [Mr. Gillis.l
United States because practically all of that type of organization in Canada is merely a subsidiary of a United States company which put up the original capital.
At page 23 of this little booklet you will find this statement. I am reading these extracts because they are relevant to the bill that is before the house at this time requesting a capital expansion. This has to do with what happened in a company that did get a large capital expansion, and did not invest it wisely. It has to do with employees' relations, tying that in with the subject I have just indicated.
As in so many other respects, Bell's reputation as a model employer does not stand up under close scrutiny. In reality, a Bell employee has little security. Until 1929. with the continued growth of the system, the number of workers steadily increased. The following year, however, although the total revenues exceeded those of 1929 by $37 million, representing the highest peak in Bell's history up to that time, the number of employees was decreased by 60,000. A. T. & T. during 1930 had greatly expanded its capital investment. Business did not increase according to anticipations and, to avoid a reduction in the net income, the workers, not the stockholders, were made to suffer for management's mistake. Throughout the depression A. T. & T. continued to pay $9 dividends per share, while its level of employment constantly declined. Between 1929 and the end of 1935, 184,600 workers were let go in one way or another. When, in 1937 another new high in A. T. & T.'s history was reached, the number of employees was 134,000 less than in 1929.
This reduced labour force failed to hamper the handling of the A. T. & T.'s increased business. Between 1930-33, a speed-up system had been inaugurated, resulting in the less, of jobs by over 30,000 persons. The introduction of the dial phone accounted for approximately 20,000 more unemployed, while a sharp decline in new construction threw an additional 40,000 out of work.
In the main, workers least able to afford it were hit by this curtailment of employment, for the lowest wage groups were those from which the discharges were made. Yet, at the same time, "the total dividend payments grew from $116,000,000 in 1929 to $168,000,000 in 1935."
Thus Bell's contribution to the unemployment of the depression years is obvious. Kqually apparent is what could have been done to alleviate it.
I read these extracts into the record merely to show that a request from the company such as we are getting at this time does not necessarily mean that that company is in a prosperous condition, or that it is going to expand its services or create more employment, or that it is going to improve its services. What I read of course took place during the depression years, but it shows that the judgment of the management in making large investments at that time was not justified. That could also be said today.
I do not think that this is the time for the British Columbia Telephone Company to come to this House of Commons and ask for the increase in capital that they are asking for. When you consider that this country is

embarking upon a defence program that is going to last for the next three years, as far as government policy at the present time is concerned, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has told the house time and time again that we are going to have to suffer and tighten our belts as far as civilian requirements are concerned; that there is going to be a shortage of material in everything that goes into ordinary consumption goods; and that at least 25 per cent of plant production, plus the raw materials in this country, are to be used for war purposes: in the light of these statements and in the light of the developing international situation, nobody in this house can rise in his place and justify the granting to this company at this time the right to increase its capital by $50 million in anticipation of increasing and expanding the services, because the government has told us time and time again that the materials are not going to be available.
In view of the fact that there are many implications in the expansion of the capital of this company, and that we have not sufficient information on the subject matter of this bill, I believe that before we adopt the principle of it on second reading the bill should go to a committee of this house for a thorough study, and that it should come back from that committee to the house, and that the sponsors of it should be prepared then to give us all the necessary information in order for us to pass the bill as it is in its present form. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce):
That Bill No. 116 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
I believe that this action is necessary at this time. I believe that that is the logical and sound thing for hon. members to do. I believe that for two reasons: One, I do not think we have the information we require to grant the request contained in this bill at this time; and, two, if we had the knowledge and the power I still question whether it is good business for hon. members at this time to be granting a lease, as it were, to companies that are going to engage in ordinary civilian activities, to give them the right to go into the market with an expanded capital, such as is suggested in this bill, and bid against the defence departments for the necessary materials that we shall require in order to bring our defence program to the fruition that is envisaged by the government. I think that is putting the company in the field to compete for materials necessary to defence at

Perhaps between now and the next time this matter comes up you might give further thought to it. I would suggest that you look up the record of the debates on the Bell Telephone Company's bill which took place in this house in 1948. On that occasion several amendments were moved. Some of them were ruled out of order, but an amendment in terms precisely similar to this one was allowed. There are citations in Beauchesne which indicate the difference that there is between the bill itself and the subject matter of the bill. A bill can be referred to a committee only after it has had second reading, but the subject matter can be referred prior to the giving of second reading to the bill, or before the principle has been approved. That course was adopted, as a matter of fact, with respect to a bill of mine some years ago, and the result was that the subject matter was discussed by the committee to which it was referred. Although no action was taken that year, the result of that discussion was that favourable action was taken a year or two later.

Mr. Chairman, I believe some questions might be asked under this Item relative to Canada's defence plans. Some time ago the Minister of Transport spoke in Quebec in regard to the general situation respecting civil aviation. My first question would be the extent to which the basic plans already existing, so far as civil aviation is concerned, are geared to the needs of the country, should an emergency arise in any part of the world, particularly as it would affect Canada.
Generally speaking, the situation as I see it is that the whole development in connection with civil aviation, or at least the major portion of it, is to permit of a rapid extension of air facilities should an emergency arise or should a war take place. It is because of the need for development and extension of civil aviation that I bring to the attention of the minister the situation in northern Saskatchewan and' in Manitoba. The hon. member for Prince Albert would no doubt make these representations if he were here but, as one of his constituents, I make them, because I know he is unavoidably absent this evening.
Great developments are taking place in northern Saskatchewan. Uranium finds in the last year have possibilities beyond anything that has ever been discovered in our country. The nearest location to those developments is the city of Prince Albert in northern Saskatchewan, and I should like to learn from the minister whether consideration has been given to extending the runways at Prince Albert so as to make them available for all-year-round traffic-in other words, to make permanent runways at that point.
At the same time I would refer to another northern airport, which is located in Manitoba at Flin Flon. Certainly Flin Flon is one airport that is necessary from a defence standpoint, as is also that at Prince Albert. Both should be in a position to provide adequate air facilities and adequate air protection for the sources of vital base metal supplies. I should like to learn from the minister in a general way something of his plans in connection with the expansion of civil aviation so that these two areas, which today do not enjoy proper facilities or proper landing fields, should be provided therewith. I am not one of those who ask for expenditures unless I believe they are necessary and will be self-liquidating. These are the two jumping-off places into the north from Manitoba and
Supply-Transport
Saskatchewan and I feel that they deserve the best air facilities that can be provided by the department.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask with regard to any conferences that have taken place during the year having to do with the development of the doctrine of freedom of the air. This may not come under this vote and I do not know under what item it would come, but I know during the past years there has been considerable discussion about the need of expanding the principle of the freedom of the air to the end that civil aviation may be properly expanded. As it is today, most nations have refused to accept the proposition that freedom of the air in so far as commercial rights are concerned should be accepted as part of the international air law.
I should like to ask the degree to which there has been expansion within the last year by Canadian Pacific Air Lines in their Pacific services. Last November there was some discussion as to whether C.P.A. would provide for calls at New Zealand in its Australia-Vancouver service. I should like the minister to give the committee a picture of the developments that have taken place during the last year and also any plans there are for the expansion of civil aviation.
There is no matter more important to our defence than the widest possible expansion of civil aviation. In making the suggestions that I have in reference to Prince Albert and Flin Flon I do so because I believe that with the development of minerals in northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba something should be done, not only to expand the commercial position of these airports but to make them available as military outposts in the event that our defences are threatened in any way.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the need for expanding the airport facilities at Regina. As I understand it, the North Star planes of the T.C.A. are unable to land at Regina. The capital city of Saskatchewan should have airport facilities sufficient to handle the largest planes. If the runways at Regina were extended perhaps one of the flights of the T.C.A. from Vancouver to Winnipeg could be dropped down at Regina and so improve the air services available to the people of southern Saskatchewan. I ask the minister to give consideration to this matter.

I should like to add a word or two to what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said with regard to the need for a civil aviation development program. The hon. member for Lake Centre has outlined

the subject so well that there is probably not much need for me to elaborate. I agree fully with the points he has made, and particularly with reference to the importance of the development of civil aviation.
When the minister replies I should like him to deal with the question of airport development. In my view there is need for an over-all program of airport development as part of a civil aviation expansion program. As the minister well knows, there are a number of airports to which I could refer in detail. However, I have taken these up with the minister by correspondence and I do not think it would be proper for me to repeat the details on this occasion. I feel that the airports in which I am interested, as well as those in which other hon. members are interested, should be handled as part of an over-all program rather than, as I think has been the case in the past, as a sort of hodgepodge development.
Grants have been made in individual cases where it has been felt they were justified, or where sufficient pressure has been put on in support of a local case. If we look at the details of one of the subsequent items we can see where a number of small grants are being made to municipalities, in some cases to assist them in the development of airports. I think this matter goes beyond what might be regarded primarily as a municipal responsibility.
I base this argument on the fact that under government policy Trans-Canada Air Lines is the only air line which is permitted to operate on the main routes in Canada. For that reason T.C.A. are in a preferred position. It is almost a foregone conclusion that there will not be many other air lines, if any, which will be able to undertake a program of airport construction of their own. In the past the railways and transportation companies have had to provide their own terminal facilities, except for those ports which come under the national harbours board where there may be some co-operation. However, generally speaking the transportation companies have had to provide their own transportation facilities, including tracks and buildings.
As we were told in the committee, T.C.A. has virtually no responsibility with respect to providing airport facilities, either runways or buildings. If the government has assumed that responsibility for T.C.A. it means that those municipalities served by T.C.A. are in an extremely fortunate position. For the reasons which I have given, it is h'ardly likely that private air lines will be able to embark on a program of airport construction which will have the effect of providing first-class
[Mr. Fulton.1
airports for those municipalities server by private lines. Therefore the case almost is that if a municipality wishes to have an airport at the present time the responsibility generally speaking is entirely that of the municipality, which is very different indeed from the history with respect to other means of transportation and communication. That is why I say it seems to me that it is essential, as one aspect of a civil aviation development program, that a sound and progressive program of airport development must be designed, laid down and carried through by progressive stages. It is admittedly a very expensive thing. I am not suggesting that we should set ourselves a target of one hundred airports a year or anything of that sort, but I am suggesting we should have a program, which could be followed through consistently, of developing airports at centres other than those served by T.C.A.
I think that the opinions I have expressed here follow logically from the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Lake Centre, with which I have said I agree, that the development of civil aviation is important not only from a commercial, but also from a defence, point of view. Certainly one of the primary necessities of the development of any program of civil aviation is a program of airport expansion. When the minister replies I wish he would make some comments on that. Perhaps I am not the original thinker here. It is likely that the department has already given some thought to this matter, and if so I would be grateful if the minister would tell us what general outline or program they have in mind.

Before the minister replies, one of the points raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre was dealt with by the Turgeon commission. In chapter 13 of their report under the heading "Air Transportation" we find that the first suggestion made to them as to airports was as follows:
That additional airstrips should be constructed in northern areas to provide better air transport between mining localities and commercial centres.
When the commission dealt with that matter they had this to say on page 261:
An interdepartmental committee was established about one year ago for the purpose of studying proposals of financial assistance for the construction of additional airports in northern areas.
Apparently there is a recognized need for the development of further airstrips in northern Canada. When the minister replies I would ask him to deal with this particular point.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time that I have been asked by

hon. gentlemen opposite to put on Hansard the pattern and the program of the department with reference to aviation developments. It was asked of me last year and the year before, but I will gladly do it again if it is the wish of the members. There is a very definite program with reference to the development of civil airports and civil aviation services together with a program developed in co-operation with officers of national defence. The object of the policy of the department is first of all to see to the progressive development of main line airports such as those which are used by T.C.A. and C.P.A. across Canada, and to permit the utilization of the most modern types of aircraft at the minimum capital outlay.
Next it is the policy to see to the development of a minimum number of international airports, and also to assist and encourage municipalities that are anxious to develop their own airports, to come to their assistance where it seems desirable that such airports should be developed, maintained and operated to standards set out by the dominion government. Then we seek to assist in the establishment of airstrips or bases feeding remote centres, such as have been referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, for the purpose of stimulating the development of Canada's natural resources. As is stated in the report, there has been in existence for some time an interdepartmental committee composed of officers of the Department of Transport, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Finance whose responsibility it is to consider the over-all program and to co-ordinate it with defence if need be, so that we have not only a program for civil development but we also are ready to assist national defence should they require additional strips or additional facilities in airports operated by the Department of National Defence.
The committee has met on a number of occasions and is responsible for the program, part of which will be seen not in this item but in the next item. I think I need hardly tell the committee that the program which can be seen in these estimates is not nearly as ambitious as the officers of the department would have wished it to be, and I speak now exclusively of civil development. Because of the priority which national defence must of necessity take over civil development, we have had to curtail very severely the expanding of civil aviation, civil airports and civil airways in the present fiscal year. Because of that it will be seen that the estimates are not nearly as high as we would have wanted them to be.

In reference to the question of stop-over rights for C.P.A. in New Zealand, which was raised in the house and which received some attention when the Prime Minister of New Zealand was here, unfortunately that has not been advanced any further. What seems to be their objection? When we were there last fall

Supply-Transport
they appeared very anxious to have direct connection with Canada. On every hand members of the house of representatives asked us whether something could not be done to assure that Canadian Pacific Air Lines would have a port of call in New Zealand. Certainly it would complete the picture and would draw us still closer to those dominions in which we have a very considerable interest. Canadian Pacific Air Lines has done a magnificent job with its air service between Vancouver and Australia, and I find it difficult to understand why any objection should be raised by the New Zealand government to landing rights there, particularly in view of the fact that, as the minister says, the government of Australia has no objection to that course being followed.

I wish I could give my hon. friend an answer to that question, but unfortunately I cannot. I do not know the reason. All I can say is that when the prime minister was here, in the discussions he had with our own Prime Minister and with me I think he too went away with the idea that there was no reason why C.P.A. should not have these rights. I understand, however, that there is a division of opinion over there as to the effect it might have on New Zealand trade, though they have been assured that stopover rights mean exactly that. Stop-over rights mean the right of a through passenger from Vancouver to Australia, let us say, to stop over in New Zealand for the matter of a week, since the trip is a weekly affair, and do not in any way mean taking away New Zealand traffic from the British commonwealth lines operating in those two dominions. Beyond that I cannot add anything. I know personally I have made the strongest representations to the representative of New Zealand in this country. He knows our position and our wishes and desires. I am sure he understands them and has explained them very carefully to his country. But I -am not able to say that it has been possible for the government of that commonwealth to grant stop-over rights.
In reference to Regina, there is an item in the next estimate dealing with the development of a strip at that airport.
What is the amount?

I was interested in the statement by the minister on the interdepartmental committee. I observe that on that committee there are representatives of the Department of National Defence, as of course everyone will agree there should be. May I ask the

minister whether that committee has referred to it any proposals of the Department of National Defence arising purely within that department for the location and construction of new airports for defence purposes, so that as far as may be possible the defence airport construction program may be integrated with the transport department airport development program?

Yes, there is consultation between the officers of national defence and our officers. There is also reference by national defence to the committee for advice on the desirability of extending a strip in an airport belonging to national defence, and the decision of the committee is later referred to the responsible minister, who takes it up with his colleagues.

There was just one other matter I wished to refer to, and it does not concern only new construction. I am referring to the airport and meteorological station-primarily the airport-at Dog Creek in British Columbia, which is situated about fifty miles from nowhere. There is a transport department meteorological station there, and during the war quite an. extensive airstrip was constructed. There is also a radio beam station. All these installations have to be maintained at very considerable expense because of the distance from any supply centre. There is a growing need for an airport at one of the other communities in the district to which I have already referred, Williams Lake. I wish the two departments would take up this matter jointly and see whether it would not be in the interests of over-all economy to move the present installation to a point where it could be serviced much more readily, and where it could form part of the eventual over-all development of an airport at Williams Lake, which is a supply and distribution centre for that part of the Cariboo country. It seems to me that might be taken up as a joint civil-defence matter for interdepartmental consideration.

I am informed that the matter has already been referred to the committee, which feels that the Dog Creek airport is a good one. While the population in that area is not very dense, still the committee feels it is an excellent airport. They have not the same opinion of Williams Lake, which is not in the same category. It is a poor airport.
At the moment.

Yes; and the Department of National Defence is not interested in the Williams Lake airport. So the committee felt

they should not disturb the present position where there is a good airport and particularly where national defence feel that there is no sound reason for moving from one to the other. If an emergency developed greater than the one which exists at the moment it might be possible to again consider Williams Lake, but at the moment that is the position.

On that point I would simply observe that obviously I would not care to disagree offhand with the view of the committee to which the minister has referred, but the fact remains that the Dog Creek installation is fifty miles from anywhere. As far as constructing any installation there is concerned, or expanding any installation, the same considerations I have referred to with respect to the existing installation of course would militate against that. I cannot go further at the moment. It is a matter on which a comparison of figures and costs perhaps should be obtained, and I shall look further into that aspect. This is the first time I have actually heard that the decision of the committee has been given. I will have to look into the matter further and perhaps pursue it at another time.

Will the minister explain the difference in the regulations applying to planes which fly, for example, into the north country and planes which fly the established routes in the southern part of Canada. I believe that a plane flying passengers into the north must carry a certain type of emergency equipment, but that is not true of ordinary passenger planes flying across the southern portion of Canada.
Shortly before Christmas last year one of the Canadian Pacific planes flying from Vancouver to Calgary crashed near Penticton. In that crash the pilot was killed, and the co-pilot was fatally injured. It took about two days for help to arrive, and in the meantime the co-pilot died. He suffered terribly until his death, as the plane did not carry emergency equipment. It apparently was not required to carry emergency equipment to any extent. I believe it had a compass, papers, chocolate, sugar, aspirins, veronal, a hatchet and matches. There were also some bandages and a few splints, but not even in sufficient quantity for the one injured person. There were also a few blankets, but all of those were required for the co-pilot. Fortunately all the passengers were saved but they suffered a great deal. I believe there should be some regulations brought into effect concerning emergency equipment on these planes. A trans-Canada plane might come down in the mountains of British Columbia or in northern Ontario. I do not understand why such planes are not required to carry some type of emergency equipment. Perhaps the thought is that if the plane crashes everyone is going to be killed anyway, and there is no use carrying anything for an emergency. In this particular case, emergency equipment would have been of great value. It might even have saved the life of the co-pilot, although I do not know that it would. Why is it there is no provision made for this type of equipment to be carried on planes flying across the settled parts of Canada?

Mr. Chairman, I remember that accident quite well. I know owing to the coolness and dexterity of the pilot all of the passengers were saved, which was quite fortunate. I should say to my hon. friend that there is no difference in the airworthiness requirements for planes flying on the international domestic main line route and those flying into the north country. Neither is there any difference in so far as emergency equipment is concerned. The Canadian Pacific plane to which reference has been made was required to carry emergency equipment. There is this difference that in

Supply-Transport
flying into the north country they take rations and so forth, which they would not normally take on main line routes.
In the case to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra refers, there was first-aid equipment on that aircraft. Over and above that, there was a qualified nurse. Canadian Pacific Air Lines, just as T.C.A., are required to carry qualified nurses on the domestic routes across Canada. They also have the first-aid equipment which is compulsory.

I would suggest that the
minister check this a little further. My informant was on the plane and was a qualified nurse. There was not sufficient equipment on that plane to look after the injured co-pilot. I believe there are regulations requiring the carrying of emergency equipment on planes flying into the north, in fact I have seen them myself. I cannot put my finger on them at the moment, but they require a certain amount of food, winter clothing and one thing and another of that type. Apparently there is nothing like that required for these ordinary passenger planes travelling across Canada. Can the minister tell us exactly what equipment has to be carried on the T.C.A. and C.P.A. planes for emergency? Could he give the committee a list of the equipment?

I will have to get the regulation and table it. I have not a copy of it here, but I am informed that there was this equipment on the plane in question. However, I would be glad, ini view of the statement made by the hon. member, to look into the matter further.

For example, there were no drugs, stretcher, food, water, axes, shovels, spades, rope, tarpaulin, heater or clothing such as socks, boots and mitts which would be required in midwinter in the case of a plane landing in the mountains. None of that material was on the plane. I am not suggesting for a moment that the Canadian Pacific did not comply with all the regulations, because I believe they did. But I would urge upon the minister to check his regulations and see whether there is not something further required for use in an emergency of that kind.

There is just one other matter. In connection with the answers given by the minister, I do not usually express my appreciation of a complete answer, but I do in this case. I think the minister went into considerable detail, and naturally such an effort as that on his part causes those who are questioning him to reciprocate. He has mentioned what is being done at Flin Flon and the additional $25,000 to be voted this year,

which will be most helpful and will provide an airport there, necessary not only for the opening of the north country but also for defence should defence become necessary.
He has stated also that, so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, there are no plans for Prince Albert. The minister suggests that consideration is being given to an airfield at Goldfields. I presume that is for the purpose of providing facilities in connection with the uranium field that is located not too distant from Goldfields. I feel that I speak for the people of Prince Albert as well as northern Saskatchewan when I say that unless the facilities in Prince Albert are made much better than they are now, anything done at Goldfields will be of little help in opening that uranium country. After all, Prince Albert is the gateway of the north in Saskatchewan. It is the nearest place to Goldfields, and there is going to be a great development there. The uranium find is supposed to be one of the most valuable in North America. Prince Albert has in operation today an airport which permits the Canadian Pacific Air Lines to land there. But it is not an airport in keeping with the responsibility that will fall on it when the northern development takes place, as we believe it will.
This request of mine for reconsideration of the laying of all-weather runways in Prince Albert will result in some expenditure, but it will be self-liquidating, and it is necessary in connection with our defence. Prince Albert is the closest to the uranium fields. The airport in Saskatoon is too far removed to be the gateway into the development that is taking place. I suggest to the minister that this matter be brought to the attention of the interdepartmental committee, and that there be established in that city runways that will permit of the development being expanded into the north, which is now in its infancy, but promises to be one of the greatest developments in our country, so far as uranium is concerned.

We operate planes of our own. In each district, I think from memory, seven or eight across Canada, we have certain planes that are required for inspection and investigation purposes. There are motor vehicles, there are snow blowers to keep the runways clear. It has been brought to my attention that there are 72 automobiles under this vote, 80 snow blowers, 451 trucks, 35 graders, 300 tractors, 26 station wagons,

Supply-Transport
9 rollers and 6 busses, all of which are required in connection with the operation of the various airports.
This would toe in the airports actually operated and owned by the department?
Yes.
As distinct from those operated by the municipalities. Is that right?
Yes.

I do not wish to press it, because the information may not be readily available. However, I did ask which airports are actually owned and operated by the government, as distinct from those operated by municipalities.
There is quite a list of those operated by the government.
You mentioned seven.
Oh no; the seven were municipally owned. There are 112 operated by the department.

It may not be easy to break that down, but I am trying to get a picture of the large airports across the country which are part of our heavy transport system. Is it possible to give a picture of those across the country operated by municipalities and those operated by the department?

I think so. For instance, Gander is operated by the department, and so are Moncton, Sydney, Dorval, Malton, Winnipeg, Ottawa, London, Windsor and Regina. The one at Calgary has been turned over by the department to the municipality. Then, those at Edmonton and Vancouver are municipally operated. Those are the three important ones of the seven mentioned a moment ago.

A few
moments ago I referred to the accommodation for passengers who have to stay overnight at Gander, when travelling by T.C.A.

I do not wish to put off the hon. member continually, so I shall deal with the matter now. Unfortunately there is no provision for the condition to which he referred. I think the only way to meet that situation would be to build a new hotel, and we find we have not the means to do that. The most important thing at Gander is to build the new airstrip which will take the heaviest planes. The next thing is to build an administration building, which is badly needed and figures largely in our plans. Unfortunately however we have not been

able to convince treasury officials that it is of such priority that it should be done now. We have convinced them however as to the airstrip. Then there are a number of other developments which must be considered before the matter the hon. member has mentioned.

I suggest there should be runways so that the heaviest planes could be accommodated because, as he knows, Gander is one of the most important airports in the world, with so many planes landing there. It would be a great mistake to neglect enlarging and straightening the runways so that they could be used by heavy planes. Do I take it that that is going to be done?

We have definite plans for
development, and the largest item in the construction vote in these estimates is for Gander.

I wish to assist the minister
and also the hon. member for St. John's West. Gander has become a kind of gateway to Canada. Often it is the only place in Canada that Americans going to New York see. I understand the facilities there are pretty ghastly. I have had some personal knowledge of that within the last couple of days. The way we handle passengers going through there is no credit to Canada.

I do think this is a subject
which has some importance, and that goes beyond the temporary convenience or otherwise of the passengers who have been compelled to wait over at Gander. Gander itself is some distance away from the larger centres of Newfoundland. Those who actually come down at that point have no facilities other than those provided at the airport.
As has been said by the hon. member who has just spoken, there is a question of public relations involved, as well as that of the comfort of the passengers. I cannot help comparing in my own mind the facilities available at either Gander or Goose with those available at Keflavik. I am not suggesting for one moment-indeed it would be inconsistent if I did so-any extravagant development, in view of certain of the things I have been saying. On the other hand there is a difference between extravagance and employing the expenditures which must be made for other things in a way that they will give some permanent facilities in these places where they are of considerable importance. Without raising this as a criticism of the past-because we all know that during

the last war certain things had to be undertaken-we do know that facilities could have been built in particular places, and that such facilities might have been used afterward, if the future expansion of aviation could have been visualized.
Having regard to the expansion that is going to take place in the air services it would seem to me that the wisdom of constructing something of the same type of accommodation as is offered by the hotel at Keflavik, at both Gander and Goose-and at Goose it would need to be on a much smaller scale than at Gander-should be given serious consideration. In the very nature of air transport, and it will be no less true with the introduction of jet aircraft, Gander and Goose will be extremely important stopping-off places under certain weather conditions. The facilities available at those points may to a very considerable extent be the deciding factor as to whether or not aircraft from the United States which constitute the major flow of transatlantic traffic will be satisfied to use those airports, or would be more inclined to expand the airports at the nearest points in the United States.
It is well known that there are now some large airports, and that there is a tendency for United States aircraft to use those airports in the United States instead of the facilities at Gander, for this very reason. Therefore I suggest that both from the practical point of view of service and that of attracting aircraft to use those airports when weather conditions demand a stop-over, consideration should be given to the location of certain defence construction projects at those places, and of a type which would be suitable both for training accommodation now and for hotel accommodation in years ahead.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss a matter which comes to my mind now, because I do not believe it could be discussed under item 523. I would hesitate to take up the time of the committee in a discussion of the matter if I felt it was one of purely local interest. I would also hesitate to suggest an expenditure of money 80709-159J
Supply-Transport
to the extent involved in connection with a matter of purely local interest. I am referring at the moment to the necessity for building a strip or airport, whatever one may call it, on which wheeled aircraft could land at Prince Rupert, British Columbia. I have said that this is not a matter of purely local interest, because I am convinced it is important to all traffic on the Pacific coast of British Columbia from Victoria at the south to Alaska at the north. It is of importance to the Pacific air traffic serving the United States and Alaska. It is essential to the east-west service from the Pacific coast in those latitudes connected with Edmonton and other points on the prairies.
Because of its value in connection with defence it is of more than local interest. I am not going to set myself up as an expert on defence matters, but I would leave with the committee the thought that if there is only one place on the mainland of the Pacific coast north of Vancouver where aircraft can be landed so as to give quick connections with the transcontinental railway and highway systems of the continent, then I suggest and submit it is of considerable importance to the country as a whole.
The situation up there is such that we are now on the main line operations of Canadian Pacific Air Lines from Vancouver. In order to get into Prince Rupert and make connections for points on the mainland of British Columbia, north of say Ocean Falls, this Canadian Pacific Air Lines plane has to set down at Sandspit on the Queen Charlotte islands when passengers and other traffic are then transferred to the mainland by a Canso-amphibian plane. The nearest point at which.-any form of wheeled aircraft can. set down on the mainland is at Terrace, some 95 miles inland from Prince Rupert which, as I shall, mention in a moment, is not regarded as suitable for traffic of this kind. The Canso service by C.P.A. is an amphibious service which lands and takes off from the water at Prince Rupert, because there is no other place at which you can land or take off.
This has been requested and demanded for some time. In so far as the area which it would serve is concerned, the request or demand is greatly aggravated at the present time by the tremendous expansion in civil activities in that part of British Columbia, which has nothing to do with the temporary and perhaps somewhat artificial stimulation that we sometimes get as a result of defence contracts.
As two examples I would mention the fact that eight miles from Prince Rupert there started operation this month the Columbia

Supply-Transport
Cellulose Company which has completed a mill at a cost of some $30 million to $35 million. This also applies-I am sticking strictly to the item-to another development which I take pride in drawing to the attention of the committee. An announcement appeared in the daily press of Canada today that in the Skeena district the Aluminum Company of Canada is to start immediately a development which will involve the expenditure of $160 million in the immediate future and of approximately $500 million before it is completed.
Projects and businesses of this ::ize cannot be served by any but the most modern, up to date and speedy transportation. For these reasons I submit that the department should give the most favourable and sympathetic consideration to the building of this airstrip.
You might say, and with reason, "Well, can't you get by with the Canso service?" I notice by recent reports in the paper that the Canso is having to make three trips a day between the island and the mainland in order to handle the traffic from Vancouver to Prince Rupert via the Queen Charlotte islands. The time will come, and I am afraid it will not be long, when the Canso aircraft in that service will have reached the stage where the Department of Transport will no longer permit them to fly in commercial service.
It is no secret that they were purchased by C.P.A. following the war at considerably less than their cost new would be. The cost of replacement with new aircraft, I say without fear of contradiction, would be so great that it would make the operation of the service prohibitive unless they were going to receive a large subsidy, which I do not think is likely.
I said that the matter was not of local concern. It has received the support of such disinterested bodies as the British Columbia aviation council, which has filed with the department a comprehensive brief on the subject. It has also the support of the associated boards of trade of central British Columbia, of the British Columbia-Yukon chamber of mines and of the Vancouver board of trade. It has also the support of practically all the local boards of trade and chambers of commerce in that district.
The site at which the residents there suggest an airport can be built feasibly is on Tugwell island, which is approximately six and a half to seven miles from the wharf at Prince Rupert and which could be served by small boats. This is all entirely protected water. I can assure the committee that I could talk for at least forty minutes outlining the details
[Mr. Applewhalte.l
of this project, but I shall not do that. At this time I am merely going to suggest that it has been reported by engineers and others familiar with the aviation business and employed in the aviation business that runways can be built of 6,000 feet, 6,600 feet,
7,000	feet, or if necessary, 8,000 feet in length.
The 6,000-foot runway can be built at a reasonable cost. The 7,000-foot runway can be built at quite a possible cost. I admit that the last 1,000 feet of runway would be expensive in proportion to the rest. The island provides sea level approaches at both ends, as do all islands. The island itself is of glacial gravel; there is no rock involved.
There is only one other point-what are the alternatives? I know what I am talking about in dealing with these. One alternative is at Sandspit, which is on an island across Hecate strait, some 80 odd miles over some of the roughest waters on the coast of British Columbia. It is considered by the leading air line there to have no value for future commercial aviation and the weather is stated to be less good on the average than at Tugwell island.
The next alternative is at Annette on the Alaskan side of the boundary. The weather there is reported definitely as being turbulent and there are no highways or railway connections.
Terrace and Kitimat are both on the mainland and have been reported by the industry as not being suitable for main line operations.
I suggest that the time has come to give this development favourable consideration, especially in view of the defence possibilities.

has a keen interest in this airport because he has brought it to our attention before. It is an airport belonging
to the Department of National Defence but operated by us on a caretaker basis. It is not felt, because of its military nature, that there should be a greater expansion of the present facilities in so far as the waiting room is concerned.

That is absurd because we do not expect to be at war for the rest of our lives.

minister to take into consideration the matter of providing suitable accommodation for people who have to make use of Torbay in travelling on planes. The minister said that the $300,000 for the Regina airport would not be nearly enough to complete the plans of the department. Would the minister give the committee some idea of what these plans are and how long it is anticipated it will take to complete them?
This item is for the construction of one runway and a taxi strip. It amounts to $300,000, and it is the first stage of the runway which will probably be completed next year.

Will the
minister indicate what the plans are for Crumlin airport at London?

The minister was going to say something about the purchase of the Vancouver airport, but apparently the only item in this vote is for the extension of a runway, or is it for a new runway?

What is the position now with regard to the dominion taking over the airport? No agreement has been reached. I received representations from a city council delegation barely two weeks ago. It means the sending of some people out there to talk things over with the city officials, but there is nothing definite at this stage.

The minister has given a general outline of some of the larger expenditures. He mentioned Regina, which is certainly necessary. I should like to secure from him a statement indicating what other expenditures are to be made for the construction or acquisition of buildings or lands and new equipment in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Before we get away too far-

Then there is an item for Swift Current of $2,500; Moose Jaw, $57,000; two additional items for Saskatoon, installation of new heating unit in garage, $6,000, and construction of vaults for runway lighting transformers, $4,000; two additional items for Swift Current, which I overlooked a moment ago, repairs to hangar roof, $20,000, and repairs to runway, $17,000; North Battleford, $3,000.

Repairs to runway and other facilities, $57,000; Yorkton, installation of fighting system, $4,500; Yorkton, construction of vaults for runway fighting transformers, $3,000. I should like to ask the minister what the plans are for the Ottawa airport and what expenditure is contemplated for this year?
TMr. Green.]

There is a substantial plan for the development of Uplands airport which has been worked out in co-operation with the Department of National Defence, arising out of the committee I mentioned a moment ago. It is a three-stage plan which provides for the construction of runways. The first stage for this year is the construction of two runways. The contract has already been awarded and it amounts roughly to $1,500,000.
That is actual construction this year?
That is right. The contract has been awarded and the contractor is now on the job.
Is any part of that to be applied to the improvement of the building used for the accommodation of passengers?

No; the whole of this
amount is for the construction of a new runway.

I was wondering if the
Minister of Transport could not save a few of these dollars and use them to build us a bridge from Morrison's island to Pembroke.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

I do not think that is out of
order. This is something we have needed for fifty years.

Are they putting in an air
service there? Coming back to the building at the airport here, I think we should have in mind facilities consistent with those ordinarily available at corresponding airports. I do not subscribe to the idea that everything should be done on an elaborate scale simply because Ottawa happens to be the capital of Canada, but it is the centre of a great many activities and particularly those related to the business of government, which uses air transportation to a greater extent each year; and the accommodation at Uplands airport is not in keeping with the importance of that airport. In the first place the building is too small. In the second place a very important consideration at a point where many passengers are meeting and changing planes is some opportunity to get meals and other things passengers require. If it is not considered advisable to actually change the building at the present time to provide proper accommodation, I do believe consideration should be given to a temporary concession of some kind for facilities of that nature. Speaking as a member with a very direct interest in that airport, and also as one who uses it considerably, I must say it is very noticeable that

its facilities are really less satisfactory than perhaps at any airport of similar importance elsewhere in this country.

I agree substantially with
what the hon. member has said in connection with the administraiion building, but I think he will agree with me that it would be foolish to spend large sums of money there when the whole plan provides for a change of site. While this three-stage plan I referred to a moment ago means the construction of air facilities, it also means that a new administration building will have to be provided. How soon it will be possible to do that I do not know, but I can assure my hon. friend that all the buildings put up by national defence will be new buildings, and we propose to set aside a site for a new administration building. Incidentally I am reminded by someone here that most of the new site is in the constituency of my colleague the hon. member for Russell.

Yes, the location is changed
slightly, but that is quite apart from the point; and the minister will have noticed that I qualified the remark I was making because of my recognition of that fact. But it is an airport of importance to the whole of this community and, I suggest, to the whole of the country. Now that the point has been raised, while I may be simply emphasizing something that has been under discussion may I seek to impress upon the department the tremendous importance of a complete co-ordination of plans between the Department of National Defence and the Department of Transport in regard to construction of this nature. I have already conceded that with the tremendous expansion during the last war it was not possible to fully anticipate the extension of air service that was going to take place. But recognizing now the increasing rate at which air transportation is becoming part of our general system of transportation in this country I would suggest that every effort be made to construct defence buildings at locations where they will be of subsequent use in the plans for civil aviation in the years ahead.
I am not suggesting that it could have been avoided in many cases, but we all know that many costly buildings were disposed of after the war for comparatively small sums because they had been erected in localities where they could not be used. No doubt that was bound to happen in some cases; nevertheless there were many instances in which airports could have been sited more effectively in relation to future civil aviation development. Right across Canada today plans have been worked out by municipalities for shorter air services,
Supply-Transport
what are described as feeder lines. Those plans should be considered in the construction carried on both by this department and by national defence. Just as one example, I know plans have been carried forward quite far for an airport that would serve the cities of Guelph, Kitchener, Waterloo and Galt. If a new airport is to be built anywhere in that area 1 would suggest that it be built in complete co-operation and co-ordination between the Department of Transport, the Department of National Defence and the municipalities, so that after its military use has become unnecessary it may be put into civilian service. I would also point out that to a substantial extent it could probably provide civilian service at the same time the military activities were being carried out. I am sure there must be similar examples right across the country, and I do believe this is a time to carry out an integration of plans between the Department of Transport, the Department of National Defence and the municipalities to a greater extent than has been the case in the past.

The minister has made the statement that no provision has been made in these estimates for the airport at London. In view of the fact that supplementary estimates will be presented; in view of the further fact that at the London airport there is a very active reserve air force squadron, and the further fact that this is a thickly populated area, I would urge that consideration be given to including sufficient funds in the supplementary estimates to make provision for the improvement of the airport at that point.
The hon. member for London has already made representations to me along those lines, and I shall be glad to give them consideration together with the representations just made.

Mr. Speaker, I have no thought of saying anything that will in any way change the pleasant mood in which the Minister of Public Works again finds himself. But I would not wish to leave the impression on Hansard that the reason for more departments not being called at this time is through any failure on the part of members on this side of the house to wish to proceed with the business of the house.
My own opinion is the time has now come for members of the house to face the fact that the business of the house could be handled much more expeditiously than it is if it were done on a more orderly basis, with knowledge in advance as to what we are going to discuss, and with some opportunity, with preparation in advance, to meet the subject we wish to discuss.
That suggestion has been made before, and I am sure many of these debates are unnecessarily lengthened by the fact that they are brought up unexpectedly and then, in the very nature of things, ideas keep occurring and new debates are precipitated through the injection of new considerations. I think that without prolonging the discussion at this time I should very properly say that if the need has now arrived for calling more departments than is customary, it is only because the business of the house is not better organized. When I say that I am not being critical directly of the Minister of Public Works, who directs the affairs of the house, but rather of the fact that we have not thus clearly defined the plans and procedure which make the business at Westminster proceed much more smoothly than it does here.
